entry.title: [BIP Proposal] Stale Tip Relay
entry.summary:
Enabling additional configuration options for network relaying features is generally unnecessary, as their effectiveness depends on being active by default. Introducing such options could complicate the process without significant benefit. If there are concerns that enabling these features would impose notable costs on node operators, it may be necessary to reconsider the overall approach to data collection rather than simply offering opt-outs.
Headers should be relayed by default across the network, as this delivers most of the intended benefits with minimal risk. Extending support to relaying entire blocks should only be considered if this feature is also enabled by default, otherwise its utility becomes questionable. The dynamics of the current public relay network form an equilibrium that discourages individual miners from deviating due to the collective infrastructure and associated costs. While tweaking job distribution is feasible when robust relay infrastructure is already in place, implementing broader changes—such as relaying stale blocks—would demand considerable coordination and investment from miners, usually for marginal expected returns.
The practical effects of these proposed changes, while likely small, should not be dismissed outright. However, rigorous analysis at this stage may be unnecessary since relaying headers alone captures the primary advantages without introducing additional complexities. Detecting transaction censorship does not provide substantial added value in this context, as observing block headers under normal stale rates offers little more information than monitoring mainchain blocks directly.
Distinguishing between near-tip block relaying and historical block sharing is important, but the discussion here focuses on real-time data propagation within the public network, making references to external repositories, such as GitHub, less relevant. Network latency figures per hop, typically around one to two seconds, align with expectations and do not significantly influence the larger argument.
Altering the default behavior of the public relay network represents a fundamental shift rather than a coordinated deviation among miners. In scenarios involving chain races, these changes can enable non-selfish miners to reorganize more quickly, although this advantage is minor compared to the gains achievable through Selfish mining strategies. Such adjustments might incentivize pool operators to refine their operational settings within the established framework, provided that they do not attempt to circumvent the public relay network or orchestrate complex attacks.
